mentions.name: Prompt injection detection library
mentions.description: This library detects prompt injection attacks at the normalisation layer, using a 10-stage deterministic pipeline (NFKD, confusable fold, leet, base64, zero-width strip, ROT13, escape sequences) that reduces all character-level evasion techniques to canonical form before any matching. Because the scan itself is code rather than a model, it is not injectable, and it is intended to replace putting another LLM in the detection path.
mentions.problem: LLM-based guardrails are themselves attack surfaces: payloads crafted with character injection techniques (homoglyphs, zero-width characters, leet, diacritics) achieve evasion rates up to 100% against classifiers that see raw tokens.

The scan itself is not injectable — it's code, not a model.

mentions.name: injection — Go prompt injection detection library
mentions.description: A Go library that detects prompt injection attacks with zero regex. It combines two curated data layers: ~35 canonical multilingual intent phrases across 8 categories (override, extraction, jailbreak, delimiter, semantic worm, agent proxy, rendering) and curated tables of evasion techniques such as Unicode confusables, leet speak mappings, LLM-specific delimiters and dangerous markup patterns. A 10-stage normalization pipeline reduces evasive text to canonical form before simple string containment and Levenshtein matching, in a ClamAV-style design where the definitions are the product. Everything ships as go:embed JSON that hot-reloads without rebuild, with no regex (no ReDoS), no API calls, no ML in the loop, and a single dependency (golang.org/x/text). It scans both LLM inputs and outputs, and the long-term goal is to make both layers community-maintained corpora consumable by any scanner regardless of language or engine.
mentions.problem: Most injection evasion makes text look different to a scanner than to the LLM — homoglyphs, leet speak, zero-width characters, base64 smuggling, ROT13 and Unicode confusables slip past pattern matchers while LLMs still read through them; regex-based scanning also carries ReDoS risk.
mentions.source_excerpt:
Prompt injection detection library in Go, zero regex.

Most injection evasion works by making text look different to a scanner than to the LLM. Homoglyphs, leet speak, zero-width characters, base64 smuggling, ROT13, Unicode confusables — the LLM reads through all of it, but pattern matchers don't.
